subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science — Physics Forces Reading
subtitle: Reading passages on forces, motion, resistance, force diagrams and practical investigation skills.
description: A reading pack for KS3 physics forces. The passages test understanding of force types, resultant forces, resistance, gravity, mass, weight and scientific investigation using source-faithful examples.

data.sourcePassage: A force is a push, pull, twist, stretch or squeeze. Forces are caused by interactions between objects and can change an object's speed, direction or shape. For example, when a person kicks a football, the foot applies a contact force to the ball. The ball speeds up, changes direction and briefly changes shape during the kick. Forces are measured in Newtons, written as N. Because forces have both size and direction, a clear scientific answer should say what type of force acts, how large it is and which direction it acts in.

questions.question: What is a force?
questions.modelAnswer: A force is a push, pull, twist, stretch or squeeze.

questions.question: What is the unit of force?
questions.modelAnswer: Newton

questions.question: Why is it not enough to say only that there is a force of 20 N?
questions.modelAnswer: A force has size and direction, so the answer should also say where the force acts, what type of force it is and which direction it acts in.

questions.question: Explain how the football example shows more than one effect of a force.
questions.modelAnswer: The kick makes the ball speed up, change direction and briefly change shape, so one interaction can affect motion and shape.

questions.question: What makes a scientific force description more precise?
questions.modelAnswer: It gives the force name or type, the size in Newtons, the direction, and the object it acts on.

data.sourceTitle: Forces That Touch and Forces at a Distance
data.targetTitle: Forces That Touch and Forces at a Distance
data.sourcePassage: Forces can be divided into contact forces and non-contact forces. A contact force acts when objects touch. Friction acts when surfaces rub or try to slide past each other. Tension acts in a stretched rope or cable. A normal contact force acts when a surface pushes back on an object. A non-contact force acts without objects touching. Gravity, magnetic forces and electrostatic forces can act at a distance. Non-contact forces can seem surprising, but they are real forces because they produce measurable effects.

questions.question: What is a contact force?
questions.modelAnswer: A contact force acts when objects touch.

questions.question: Which force is non-contact?
questions.modelAnswer: Gravity

questions.question: Why is tension a contact force?
questions.modelAnswer: Tension acts through a stretched rope, string, chain or cable that is touching the object it pulls.

questions.question: Why should non-contact forces still be treated as real forces?
questions.modelAnswer: They can act at a distance and produce measurable effects, such as gravity pulling objects down or a magnet attracting steel.

questions.question: A book rests on a table. Name the two main forces acting and classify each one.
questions.modelAnswer: Weight acts downwards and is caused by gravity, a non-contact force. The normal contact force from the table acts upwards and is a contact force.

data.sourcePassage: The resultant force is the single overall force after all forces on an object have been combined. When forces act in the same direction, add them. When forces act in opposite directions, subtract the smaller force from the larger force. If equal forces act in opposite directions, the resultant force is 0 N and the forces are balanced. Balanced forces do not always mean an object is stationary. A stationary object stays stationary, but a moving object continues at steady speed in a straight line. Unbalanced forces can make an object speed up, slow down, change direction or change shape.

questions.question: What is the resultant force?
questions.modelAnswer: It is the single overall force after all forces on an object have been combined.

questions.question: What is the resultant force when equal opposite forces act?
questions.modelAnswer: 0 N

questions.question: A push of 50 N acts right and friction of 20 N acts left. What is the resultant force?
questions.modelAnswer: The resultant force is 30 N to the right because 50 N minus 20 N equals 30 N and the larger force acts right.

questions.question: Why is it a misconception to say balanced forces always mean an object is not moving?
questions.modelAnswer: Balanced forces mean no change in motion. The object may be stationary, or it may already be moving at steady speed in a straight line.

questions.question: Explain how unbalanced forces can change motion in three different ways.
questions.modelAnswer: An unbalanced resultant force can speed an object up if it acts in the direction of motion, slow it down if it acts opposite to motion, or change direction if it acts sideways.

data.sourceTitle: Friction, Air Resistance and Water Resistance
data.targetTitle: Friction, Air Resistance and Water Resistance
data.sourcePassage: Friction is a contact force that opposes sliding or attempted sliding between surfaces. It can be useful, such as when shoes grip the ground or bike brakes slow wheels. It can also be unwanted because moving machine parts can wear down and transfer energy by heating. Air resistance opposes motion through air and water resistance opposes motion through water. These resistance forces become larger when an object moves faster, has a larger surface area or has a less streamlined shape. Streamlined shapes reduce resistance in fluids.

questions.question: What does friction oppose?
questions.modelAnswer: Friction opposes sliding or attempted sliding between surfaces.

questions.question: Which shape reduces resistance in fluids?
questions.modelAnswer: Streamlined

questions.question: Give one useful and one unwanted effect of friction.
questions.modelAnswer: Friction is useful for grip when walking or braking, but it can be unwanted when machine parts wear down or become hot.

questions.question: Why does opening a parachute increase air resistance?
questions.modelAnswer: Opening the parachute greatly increases surface area, so it pushes against more air and produces a larger upward air resistance force.

questions.question: Explain why air resistance rises more quickly at higher speeds.
questions.modelAnswer: A faster object collides with more air particles each second, so the force from the air becomes greater.

data.sourcePassage: A student can investigate how surface type affects the force needed to move a block. The independent variable is the surface type, such as smooth plastic, wood, carpet or sandpaper. The dependent variable is the force needed to pull the block, measured in Newtons with a force meter. Control variables include using the same block, same added mass, same pulling speed, same force meter and same distance each time. Repeats make results more reliable and help identify anomalous results. In one set of results, sandpaper readings of 4.8 N, 7.9 N and 5.0 N included an anomalous 7.9 N reading, so the test should be repeated.

questions.question: What is the independent variable in this investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the surface type.

questions.question: What instrument measures the force needed to pull the block?
questions.modelAnswer: Force meter

questions.question: Name two control variables from the investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: Possible control variables include the same block, same added mass, same pulling speed, same force meter and same distance pulled.

questions.question: Why are repeats useful in this investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeats improve reliability and help identify anomalous results that do not fit the pattern.

questions.question: Why is 7.9 N likely to be anomalous in the sandpaper readings?
questions.modelAnswer: It is much higher than the other sandpaper readings of 4.8 N and 5.0 N, so the block may have caught or the student may have jerked the force meter.
